blocks.text: Patient discloses domestic abuse
AMaC MRCP PACES23 | Round 5 | R5-341 | Station 4: Communication and Ethics | 10 minutes | Criteria are AMaC educational, not an official PACES mark scheme | 14 October 2026

A 29-year-old attends with recurrent unexplained injuries. When interviewed alone they say their partner has been violent and controls their phone. They fear going home and ask you not to tell anyone.

Start with privacy, immediate safety and control over disclosure. Never promise absolute secrecy, pressure police involvement, or send unsafe written information home.
Unsafe shortcut: Capacitous adults generally direct their information-sharing unless law or overriding risk justifies disclosure. Risks to children or others require separate safeguarding assessment; do not mechanically disclose every adult disclosure to police.

rows: “First, I want to make sure everyone is safe.”
Ask whether the perpetrator is nearby, threats to kill, strangulation, weapons, escalating violence, stalking, sexual harm, pregnancy and whether children or vulnerable adults are exposed.
“I will explain what you can choose and when I must act.”

blocks.text: Patient: “My partner pushed me, but please do not tell anyone.” Initially minimise injuries. If spoken to alone, reveal increasing intimidation and a child at home who witnessed an incident. Ask: “Will you call my partner?”

Question 1. What immediate safety questions should you ask privately?
Expected answer 1. Speak alone, ask about immediate danger and injuries, and assess children or other people at risk.
Question 2. How do you respond to a domestic abuse disclosure?
Expected answer 2. Offer a non-judgemental response, explore the patient's priorities and establish safe methods of contact.
Question 3. What are the limits of confidentiality?
Expected answer 3. Explain confidentiality honestly, including circumstances where proportionate safeguarding disclosure may be needed.
Question 4. How would you arrange further protection and referral?
Expected answer 4. Document facts, offer domestic-abuse service/safeguarding referral, and arrange safe follow-up without forcing disclosure.
Question 5. What do you do if the suspected perpetrator enters?
Expected answer 5. Curveball: The alleged abuser returns to the room; avoid revealing private disclosures and prioritise immediate safety.
[R1] Pass: Offers private conversation away from accompanying person | High-performance: Checks safe interpreter and means of contact

FAIL — CANDIDATE: “I will ring your partner to hear both sides.” [Critical: increased risk and confidentiality breach.]

PASS — CANDIDATE: “I believe you. Are you safe to go home? Is anyone else, including a child, at risk? We can speak privately and arrange specialist domestic abuse support. I will explain when confidentiality may need to be shared for safety.”

HIGH-PERFORMANCE — CANDIDATE: “I will assess immediate danger, children and other dependants, discuss safe contact and a tailored safety plan, seek safeguarding advice, share only necessary information where legally justified, and document your wishes without pressuring you to leave.”

Case-specific unsafe responses: Questions patient in front of suspected abuser; Ignores immediate danger and dependent children; Promises absolute secrecy regardless of serious risk; Insists on police reporting as the only possible route; Automatically tells partner/family or refuses all safeguarding escalation; Creates unsafe messages or discharge papers visible to abuser. A serious safety failure requires escalation under the station-specific clinical protocol; the above are educational descriptors, not official PACES marking rules.

“Thank you for telling me. Are you safe to return home today?”
“Would it be possible to speak privately about what has happened and any children or other people at risk?”
“I will explain confidentiality and its limits, and we can agree a safe support and referral plan together.”
“I want to establish immediate risk and a safe communication plan.”
“I will document why I shared or did not share information and consult the relevant safeguarding lead.”

Start with privacy, immediate safety and control over disclosure. Never promise absolute secrecy, pressure police involvement, or send unsafe written information home. Validate without blame; ask about immediate danger and safe contact. Offer specialist domestic abuse advocacy and local safeguarding team, use DASH or local structured risk assessment and high-risk MARAC pathway where indicated; agree a safe plan and factual secure documentation.
